long: Search technique that understands the meaning and intent of the query, rather than just matching literal keywords.
example: Searching for «something to sit on» and finding «chair» or «sofa» even if they don't contain those words.

short: NLP technique that identifies emotions or attitudes (positive, negative, neutral) in text.
long: NLP technique that identifies emotions or attitudes (positive, negative, neutral) in text.
example: Analyzing customer opinions on social media to detect reputation crises.

short: Unauthorized use of AI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) by employees without IT or compliance approval.
long: Unauthorized use of AI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) by employees without IT or compliance approval.
example: Employees pasting customer data into ChatGPT without realizing they are violating internal policies.

short: Converting speech to text (STT) and text to speech (TTS) using AI models.
long: Converting speech to text (STT) and text to speech (TTS) using AI models.
example: Automatically transcribing meetings or creating voice assistants.

short: Artificially generated data that mimics the statistical properties of real data, used when real data is scarce or to protect privacy.
long: Artificially generated data that mimics the statistical properties of real data, used when real data is scarce or to protect privacy.
example: Creating realistic but fake customer histories to train scoring models without violating GDPR.

short: Fixed initial instruction that defines the model’s role, tone, rules and personality throughout the entire conversation.
long: Fixed initial instruction that defines the model’s role, tone, rules and personality throughout the entire conversation.
example: «You are an internal finance assistant of an IBEX 35 company. Never give investment advice. Always reply in Spanish and with 2025-updated data».

short: Hyperparameter that controls randomness in model responses (0 = deterministic, 1 = very creative).
long: Hyperparameter that controls randomness in model responses (0 = deterministic, 1 = very creative).
example: Temperature 0 for legal answers; 0.7–0.9 for creative campaign copywriting.

short: Process of splitting text into smaller units (tokens) that the model can process, such as words or subwords.
long: Process of splitting text into smaller units (tokens) that the model can process, such as words or subwords.
example: The word 'tokenization' might split into ['token', 'ization'].

short: Smallest unit of text processed by a model, which can be a word or a fragment.
long: Smallest unit of text processed by a model, which can be a word or a fragment.
example: The cost of using ChatGPT is measured in tokens processed.

short: Model ability to decide when and how to call external tools (APIs, databases, calculators) instead of trying to answer everything itself.
long: Model ability to decide when and how to call external tools (APIs, databases, calculators) instead of trying to answer everything itself.
example: An assistant that queries the ERP to give real-time stock of an order instead of hallucinating it.

short: Sampling method that only considers tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p (usually 0.9–0.95).
long: Sampling method that only considers tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p (usually 0.9–0.95).
example: Combine temperature 0.8 + top-p 0.95 for coherent but non-repetitive answers.

short: Technique that reuses a pre-trained model on a related task to speed up training on a new problem.
long: Technique that reuses a pre-trained model on a related task to speed up training on a new problem.
example: Adapting a general image model to specific medical diagnosis.

short: Architecture that allows efficient parallel processing of sequences such as text.
long: Architecture that allows efficient parallel processing of sequences such as text.
example: Foundation of most current generative models.

short: Degree to which the functioning of an algorithmic decision system can be explained and understood.
long: Degree to which the functioning of an algorithmic decision system can be explained and understood.
example: Detailing recommendation criteria in a job platform.

short: Ability to know how, with which data and with which versions a model was trained and changed.
long: Ability to know how, with which data and with which versions a model was trained and changed.
example: Demonstrating compliance during regulatory audits.

short: Situation where a model is too simple and fails to capture underlying patterns in the data, leading to poor performance on both training and test data.
long: Situation where a model is too simple and fails to capture underlying patterns in the data, leading to poor performance on both training and test data.
example: A linear model that poorly predicts complex variations in sales data.

short: Model that learns to compress data into a latent space and then reconstruct it, useful for generation and dimensionality reduction.
long: Model that learns to compress data into a latent space and then reconstruct it, useful for generation and dimensionality reduction.
example: Generating product design variations while maintaining key features.

short: Database optimized to store embeddings and perform similarity search.
long: Database optimized to store embeddings and perform similarity search.
example: Using Chroma or Pinecone in corporate semantic search systems.

short: Transformer-based architecture applied to images by splitting them into patches and processing them as sequences, often outperforming CNNs.
long: Transformer-based architecture applied to images by splitting them into patches and processing them as sequences, often outperforming CNNs.
example: Modern image classification models that use attention instead of convolutions.

short: Ability of a model to handle tasks without specific prior examples.
long: Ability of a model to handle tasks without specific prior examples.
example: ChatGPT solving a question that was not directly seen during training.

short: A specific function or capability that an AI agent can execute to perform a task.
long: A specific function or capability that an AI agent can execute to perform a task.
example: A calendar search 'skill' that allows an agent to check availability and schedule meetings.

short: Open protocol that standardizes how AI models connect with data sources and tools.
long: An open protocol that standardizes how AI models connect with local or remote data sources and tools, enabling different applications and models to exchange context information uniformly.
example: Connecting a coding IDE to a proprietary database via MCP so the AI can query table schemas.

short: A model that uses additional inference-time computation to solve tasks requiring multiple steps or more careful deliberation.
long: An AI model optimized for solving complex problems through additional inference-time computation, for example by generating and evaluating possible solutions. It may produce explanations, but these do not necessarily reveal the model’s full internal process.
example: An assistant spends additional inference time checking a mathematical proof before answering.

short: Design pattern where the AI iterates, searches for tools, and reflects to complete a task.
long: A design pattern in which the AI does not generate a response in a single step, but follows a cycle of planning, executing with tools, reflecting on the results, and correcting until the task is complete.
example: A workflow where an agent writes code, attempts to execute it, analyzes the error, searches documentation, and fixes the code autonomously.

short: Open standard that lets distinct AI agents discover capabilities, exchange information, and coordinate tasks.
long: A2A defines a common way for agents built with different platforms or frameworks to communicate and collaborate. It complements protocols such as MCP, which connect AI applications to tools and data sources.
example: A purchasing agent delegates an inventory check to an agent from another provider through A2A.

short: Knowledge and skills needed to understand AI, use it thoughtfully, and recognize its opportunities and risks.
long: AI literacy combines a basic understanding of how AI systems work and where their limits lie with the ability to use them and assess their outputs appropriately for the context.
example: Training staff to recognize when a generated answer needs verification before it is shared.

short: An AI system’s ability to observe an interface and operate it through actions such as clicking and typing.
long: In computer use, a model interprets screenshots or the visible state of an interface and performs actions such as moving a cursor, clicking, or entering text. Actions may require permissions and oversight because they can affect real applications.
example: An agent reads an invoice in a web portal and copies its amount into an accounting system.

short: Computational resources a model uses while generating an answer, in addition to those used during training.
long: Increasing inference-time compute can let a model explore, generate, or check more options before answering. It may improve some results, but also increases latency and cost and does not guarantee correctness.
example: A model uses additional computation to compare several solutions to a programming problem.

short: Temporary memory that reuses attention values already computed during sequential token generation.
long: In Transformer models, the KV cache retains keys and values for earlier tokens so they do not need to be recomputed at every generation step. It reduces repeated computation and latency at the cost of memory, especially with long contexts or many concurrent requests.
example: A generation service caches prior states to produce the next part of a response faster.

short: A systematic process for measuring whether a model meets quality, usefulness, and safety criteria for an intended use.
long: Evaluation combines tests, datasets, metrics, and human review to estimate a model’s capabilities and limitations on specific tasks. Results depend on how tests are designed and should be interpreted in the context of use.
example: Compare two models on representative customer support cases and review their errors before deployment.

short: A technique that reuses processing for repeated input prefixes to reduce inference time or cost.
long: Prompt caching lets a platform recognize identical or reusable parts of earlier requests, such as long instructions or reference documents. Availability, retention, and savings depend on the provider and configuration.
example: An application reuses the instructions and product manual included in many customer support queries.

short: An inference method that speeds up generation by proposing multiple tokens with a fast model and checking them with the main model.
long: A draft model predicts a short sequence of tokens and the main model verifies which ones to accept. When effective, more tokens are generated per step without changing the output the main model would have produced, though gains depend on model compatibility and workload.
example: A small model proposes the next words and the production model validates them in parallel.

short: Verifiable information about the origin and edits of content generated or modified with AI.
long: Provenance may include signed metadata, credentials, or records indicating who created content and which tools or edits were involved. It helps assess an item’s history, but can be lost when the file is shared and does not by itself prove the content is true.
example: A photograph includes credentials showing it was created with a generative tool and later cropped.

short: Increasing inference resources to improve a model’s performance on a specific task.
long: Test-time scaling allocates more computation, attempts, or search during inference, for example by generating several solutions and selecting one. Benefits depend on the task and method, and may increase costs or even worsen some results.
example: A system generates several candidate answers to a logic problem, checks them, and returns the most consistent one.

short: A model that combines visual perception and language understanding to produce actions, often for robots.
long: A vision-language-action model connects images or video with instructions and executable actions. It can translate commands into robot movements, but requires testing and controls suited to the physical environment where it operates.
example: A robot interprets “pick up the red cup” through its camera and plans the required movements.

short: Execution layer that turns a model into an agent by managing context, tools, state, and actions.
long: An agent harness coordinates the loop between a model and its environment: it prepares context, executes tool calls, maintains or updates state, and applies limits and controls. Its design influences agent behavior alongside the model.
example: The harness receives a request, lets the model query an API, validates the proposed action, and returns the result to the model.

short: Testing an agent on multi-step tasks to measure outcomes, tool use, and behavior during execution.
long: Agent evaluation examines not only the final answer, but also whether the agent completes the task, chooses suitable tools, respects limits, recovers from errors, and avoids unintended actions. Tests should reflect the intended environment and risks.
example: Test a support agent on representative requests and check both its answer and the queries and changes it made in the CRM.

short: The design and management of information supplied to a model to help it complete a task.
long: Context engineering selects, organizes, and updates instructions, retrieved data, history, tools, and other elements the model receives during a task. In agentic systems, context can change between steps; its quality and relevance affect results.
example: A research agent receives the question, relevant retrieved documents, and an updated summary of its earlier findings.

short: The practice of designing and improving the execution infrastructure, controls, and context around an AI agent.
long: Harness engineering works on an agent’s runtime layer: its tool loop, context, state, permissions, error handling, and evaluation. It aims to make the overall system more reliable and observable without relying only on changing or retraining the model.
example: A team adjusts tool permissions, action logging, and error recovery for its coding agent.

short: Repeated cycle in which an agent receives context, decides or calls tools, observes results, and continues until a task is completed or stopped.
long: The agent loop connects a model with its environment across multiple steps: it prepares the input, executes a decision or tool call, incorporates the result, and decides whether to continue, finish, or ask for help. Its limits include stop criteria, time, and number of actions.
example: An agent queries an API, reviews the result, and searches again if it still lacks enough information.

short: Designing repeatable work cycles that let an agent make progress, check results, and correct or stop according to defined criteria.
long: Loop engineering organizes how an agent works iteratively: breaking goals into tasks, supplying context and tools, checking evidence, handling errors, and deciding when to retry, continue, or stop. The term is recent and is used especially for agentic software development workflows; its practices overlap with harness engineering and agentic workflow design.
example: An agent changes code, runs tests, analyzes failures, and repeats the cycle until acceptance criteria are met or a limit is reached.
